lead: Three tools close the edit-run-inspect loop. VS Code is the editor: it holds your files, runs a terminal and pauses code at breakpoints. Git records the history of those files as commits, so you can go back or work on a branch. The browser console and DevTools report what actually happened: JavaScript errors, and the URL, method, status and size of every request. Used together they replace guesses with measurements. This chapter wires the three into one habit; deployment and branching strategy come later.
prereq: You need 1.3 for who renders and who answers, and 1.4 for the status codes and headers you will read in the Network panel.

sections.h3: VS Code: edit, run and pause in one window

blocks.text: Visual Studio Code is a free source-code editor from Microsoft. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. You open a folder as a workspace; the file explorer on the left lists that folder, and a click opens a file in a tab.

The editor is not a compiler and not a web server. It does not build or serve your page by itself. It gives you an integrated terminal (Ctrl+`) that runs the same commands a shell would: node app.js, python manage.py, git status. The output appears beside your code, so you never switch windows.

Extensions add language support. Live Server serves a folder over HTTP and reloads the browser on each save. Prettier reformats code. ESLint marks JavaScript problems as you type. Extensions run with your permissions, so install only what you need.

A breakpoint is a red dot set in the gutter left of a line number. Start the debugger with F5 and execution pauses at that line. The Variables panel shows the variables in the current scope and the scopes above it; the debug console lets you evaluate any expression you type. Step over runs the next line without entering a function; step into goes inside it. You read the real value instead of guessing with print statements.

sections.h3: Git: three places a file can live

blocks.text: Git is a version control system. A repository is a folder Git watches, plus a hidden .git directory that stores every saved version. Inside it a file passes through three places.

items: The working tree is the folder as you see it, including your unsaved-in-Git edits.
The staging area, also called the index, is the set of changes chosen for the next save.
The repository is the permanent record: the chain of commits.

blocks.text: git status prints which file is in which place. Two commands move a file forward. git add app.css copies the current content into the staging area. git commit -m "fix navbar colour" records the staged content as a commit, carrying a hash id, the author, the time and the message.
A commit is local. It writes to .git on your own disk and touches no network. That is the most examined point in this chapter: commit saves, push uploads.

A branch is a movable name pointing at one commit. git branch login creates one, git switch login moves onto it, and git merge login, run from main, brings those commits into main. A remote is a copy of the repository on another machine. git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/yourrepo.git names that copy origin; git push -u origin main uploads your commits; git pull downloads and merges other people's.
.gitignore is a plain text file of patterns Git must not track: node_modules/, .env, *.log. Secrets and generated files then stay out of history.

sections.h3: Browser DevTools: what the page really did

blocks.text: DevTools is built into every major browser; F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I opens it. It attaches to the page you are on and reports facts, not intentions.

head: Panel
Question it answers
rows: What is the DOM now, and which CSS rule wins?
Which JavaScript error or log message appeared?
Which URL, method, status, size and time per request?
Which cookies and storage keys are stored?

blocks.text: Elements shows the live DOM, the tree the browser built from your HTML after JavaScript changed it. Editing a value in the Styles pane updates the page at once, which is useful for trying a colour before typing it into the CSS file.
Console lists your console.log output and every uncaught JavaScript error, with file and line. A red line here is the fastest explanation for a button that does nothing.

Network records every request with its URL, method (GET, POST), status code, transferred size and time. Tick Disable cache while testing. A row marked (from cache) shows 0 bytes transferred. A 304 response transfers only headers, and a 404 often carries a small error body; their transferred size is a few hundred bytes at most, small enough to count as 0 in exam arithmetic but not literally zero. So the total is not the page weight.
Application shows what the site stored on your machine: cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage and service workers.

figure.caption: git add moves the 2 changed files to staging, git commit saves them in the local .git folder, and only git push uploads them. In DevTools only index.html and app.js cross the network, 4 + 30 = 34 KB, while app.css comes from cache and the favicon fails with 404.

spec.aria: Four git places in a row joined by git add, git commit and git push; below, a DevTools network table lists index.html 4 KB, app.css from cache 0 KB, app.js 30 KB and favicon.ico 404, total 34 KB.

examples.question: A page loads index.html of 4 KB, app.css of 12 KB and app.js of 30 KB. app.css is already in the browser cache; the other two are downloaded. git status shows app.css modified and logo.svg untracked. The DevTools Console shows a 404 for /favicon.ico. Find (a) the bytes transferred, (b) the number of files to stage, and (c) whether git commit uploads the code.
steps: Transferred size counts only bytes that crossed the network. index.html is downloaded: 4 KB.
app.css is served from cache, so it contributes 0 KB to transferred size even though the page uses it.

Total transferred = 4 KB + 30 KB = 34 KB. The 404 for favicon.ico transfers only headers and possibly a tiny error body, small enough to count as 0 KB in exam arithmetic, but not literally zero. It is still a failed request worth fixing.
git status lists two changes: app.css is modified (tracked) and logo.svg is new (untracked). Both must be staged, so run git add app.css logo.svg.
git commit -m "..." writes a new commit into the local .git directory only. Nothing leaves the machine until git push origin main runs.
So commit does not upload; push does.
examples.answer: 34 KB transferred (4 KB HTML + 30 KB JS; the cached CSS and the failed favicon are counted as 0 bytes), 2 files to stage, and the commit stays local until a push.

traps: git commit saves to the local repository only. It does not upload. Without git push the teammate sees nothing.

Transferred size in Network is not page weight. Files served from cache show 0 bytes; a 304 transfers only headers, and a 404 may carry a tiny error body, so count them as 0 in exam arithmetic but not as a literal measurement. The total is smaller than the sum of the file sizes.
Saving a file in the editor is not a commit. Ctrl+S writes the working tree; git add copies to staging; git commit records it. Three separate steps.
A 404 is a completed HTTP exchange: the server answered. It is not 'no response' and it is not a JavaScript syntax error, which would appear in Console as a different message.
.gitignore stops untracked files only. A file already committed stays tracked; you must run git rm --cached to untrack it.

quiz.q: Name the three places a file can be in Git, in the order it moves through them.
quiz.a: Working tree, then staging area (index), then repository (commit history).

quiz.q: Which DevTools panel shows status codes and transferred size, and which shows cookies?
quiz.a: Network shows status and transferred size; Application shows cookies and storage.

quiz.q: Why can Network show 0 bytes for a CSS file the page is clearly using?
quiz.a: For a cache hit no body crosses the network, so the row shows 0 bytes. A 304 revalidation transfers only headers, small enough to count as 0 in exam arithmetic. The file still applies to the page; transferred size counts downloaded body bytes, not page weight.

quiz.q: A page loads index.html 5 KB, style.css 8 KB, bundle.js 45 KB and one 404 favicon. style.css is cached. Find the transferred bytes.
quiz.a: Downloaded: index.html 5 KB + bundle.js 45 KB. Cached style.css = 0 KB. The 404 is counted as 0 KB in exam arithmetic; it may carry a tiny error body. Total transferred = 5 + 45 = 50 KB.

quiz.q: You changed two files, app.css and logo.svg. Write the two Git commands that record them without uploading.
quiz.a: git add app.css logo.svg, then git commit -m "message". Both act on the local repository; nothing is uploaded.

quiz.q: A developer commits and tells a teammate the fix is online. The teammate still sees the bug. Explain.
quiz.a: The commit exists only in the local .git directory. The remote repository has no such commit, so the teammate's clone and the deployed site are unchanged. The missing step is git push origin main, followed by a fresh fetch or pull on the other side.

quiz.q: Compare a breakpoint with a console.log for finding why a variable is wrong.
quiz.a: A console.log prints one frozen value at the place you wrote it and needs a save-and-reload cycle for every change. A breakpoint pauses execution so you can inspect all variables, step forward line by line and change a value to test a hypothesis, all without editing the source.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, VS Code Remote and Dev Containers let you edit code that runs on another machine, so the editor window and the runtime are separate. Source maps let DevTools show your original JavaScript names even after a build tool has minified the file. Git hooks and CI pipelines run tests automatically on every push, which is why commit messages are written carefully.
